content: A Baker's cyst, also referred to as a popliteal cyst, is a non-cancerous swelling that develops behind the knee joint. It is named after Dr. William Morrant Baker, the surgeon who first described it. Etiology In adults, Baker's cysts typically result from various forms of knee arthritis or cartilage injuries, particularly meniscal tears. They can also be associated with Lyme disease. However, in children, Baker's cysts are not indicative of underlying joint disease. These cysts form between the tendons of the medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle and the semimembranosus muscle, located posterior to the medial femoral condyle. Under certain conditions, the synovial sac of the knee joint may bulge posteriorly into the popliteal space (the area behind the knee). When this bulge becomes large enough, it can be felt as a cystic mass. Most Baker's cysts maintain a direct connection with the synovial cavity of the knee, although some may become pinched off. A ruptured Baker's cyst can cause sudden pain behind the knee, calf pain, and swelling in the calf muscles. Diagnosis Diagnosis is primarily made through physical examination. Baker's cysts are more visible when the patient is standing with knees fully extended and are easier to palpate when the knee is partially flexed. Ultrasound is used to confirm the diagnosis. If there is no suspicion of a popliteal artery aneurysm, aspiration of synovial fluid from the cyst may be performed cautiously. MRI imaging can also confirm the presence of a Baker's cyst. A ruptured cyst may mimic symptoms of thrombophlebitis or deep vein thrombosis (DVT), such as calf pain, swelling, and redness. In such cases, urgent blood tests and ultrasonography are necessary to rule out DVT. Although rare, a Baker's cyst can compress vascular structures, leading to leg edema or even a true DVT. Treatment Baker's cysts often do not require treatment unless they cause symptoms. Rest and leg elevation are usually sufficient. If needed, the cyst can be aspirated to reduce its size, followed by an injection of corticosteroids to decrease inflammation. Surgical removal is reserved for cases where the cyst causes significant discomfort. A ruptured cyst is managed with rest, leg elevation, and corticosteroid injections into the knee. Prolotherapy, a treatment used at the Mayo Clinic since 2005, has shown promise in managing Baker's cysts and other musculoskeletal conditions. In children, Baker's cysts almost always resolve on their own over time and rarely require surgical excision. Symptomatic Relief Cryotherapy Applying ice packs is an effective way to manage pain caused by a Baker's cyst. Ice should not be applied directly to the skin but should be separated by a thin cloth. Cooling packs can also be used, but the total application time should not exceed 15 minutes at a time. Medication Over-the-counter medications, such as acetaminophen (Tylenol) or anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen or naproxen, can help alleviate pain. In some cases, stronger non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be prescribed by a physician. Heat Heat therapy, such as using a heating pad on a low setting for 10–20 minutes, may provide pain relief if used according to instructions. Bracing A knee brace can provide support and reduce pain by stimulating nerve fibers, creating a sensation of joint stability. If only support is needed, a simple elastic bandage is recommended. However, braces may compress the back of the knee, where the cyst is most tender, potentially causing discomfort. Rest and Specific Exercises Certain activities, such as squatting, kneeling, heavy lifting, climbing, and running, can strain the knee and exacerbate pain. Avoiding these activities can help prevent discomfort. However, specific exercises, such as those aimed at stretching and strengthening the quadriceps or patellar ligament, may alleviate pain. A physiotherapist can provide guidance on appropriate exercises.
